title: What If Zombies Took Over Tomorrow?

lines.text: The dead are walking. Now what?
It's seven a.m. tomorrow. You're making coffee when your phone buzzes on the counter. Then again. And again. An outbreak at a city hospital, and one word on every screen. Lockdown.
You go to the window. A car alarm is wailing, someone is screaming, and a man in a torn shirt is walking slowly down the middle of your street.
He doesn't flinch at the noise. He walks toward it. In this story, they are slow, they follow sound and light, and one bite is all it takes.
This is The Survivometer. We'll live through it hour by hour, and at the end, we'll see your odds of making it one full year.
visual: HOUR BY HOUR. ONE FULL YEAR.

lines.text: Right now, it's a coin flip. Fifty percent. Every small decision from here moves the needle.
Eight a.m. Someone is pounding on your door. It's your neighbor from across the hall. You call his name. He doesn't answer. He just keeps pounding.
You don't open it. You press your back against the door and wait until the pounding fades down the hallway.
Outside, the whole street has the same idea. Car doors slam, engines start, and everyone grabs their keys and drives.
But a city of a million people can't squeeze through a handful of roads. Within an hour, the highway is a parking lot, and the dead are walking between the cars.
You could join them. Most people do. You decide to stay put.
You drag the bookshelf in front of the door, close the curtains, and fill every pot, bottle and bathtub you own while the water still runs.
Then you sit on the kitchen floor and count what you have. Food for about a week, some painkillers, and a drawer full of half dead batteries.
And there's a reserve most people forget. The water heater in your closet holds about forty gallons of clean water. Staying put pushes your odds to fifty five.
One p.m. Something has changed, and it takes you a moment to notice. The sirens have stopped. Not because it's over. Because no one is left to answer the calls.
From your window you start counting. Ten on your block. Then thirty. Every car alarm and every scream pulls more of them toward the noise.
Your phone still shows one bar, but not for long. Cell towers run on backup batteries that typically last between two and eight hours.
visual: Sources: FCC backup power rule, industry reports

lines.text: So you use it while you can. One message to the people you love. Where you are, and where you'll meet if the phones die.
Then you switch the phone to silent. Through a thin door, a ringtone is a dinner bell.
visual: A RINGTONE IS A DINNER BELL

lines.text: You write the important numbers on paper and download offline maps. Your GPS doesn't need cell towers. It listens to satellites, and it keeps working long after the network is gone.
Quiet, prepared, and still unseen. Your odds tick up to fifty eight.
Seven forty p.m. The TV flickers, the fridge goes quiet, and the lights go out.
Power plants need fuel deliveries and people at the controls. Energy analysts who gamed out this exact scenario estimated that fossil fuel plants would start shutting down within about 24 hours.
visual: UNTIL FOSSIL PLANTS START TO TRIP

lines.text: Then it falls like dominoes. No gas pumps. No card readers, so suddenly only cash works. No refrigeration, and no elevators.
That night, the city is darker than it has been in a hundred years. And in the dark, any light is a beacon.
Across the street, a family lights candles and a camping lantern. You watch the warm glow in their window. Within an hour, a crowd of the dead is pressed against their front door.
You look down at the box of matches in your hand. Then you put it back in the drawer.
You sit in the dark, you whisper when you have to talk, and you wait for morning.
Staying dark keeps you at sixty percent. That one candle would have dropped you to thirty five.
Day three. You turn the kitchen tap. It coughs out a little air, and then nothing.
City water pressure depends on electric pumps. The water towers bought you about a day, and now they're empty too.
You can last weeks without food, but only about three days without water. The bathtub is almost empty, and the water heater won't last forever.
The grocery store two blocks away is your best chance. A typical city holds only about three days of fresh food, so whatever is left is going fast.
visual: OF FRESH FOOD IN A TYPICAL CITY
Source: Evan Fraser, University of Guelph

lines.text: You could wait for the cover of night. But think about how they hunt.
At night, you'd need a flashlight, and a flashlight is a beacon. So you go at noon, when you can see them first.
You move low between the parked cars. Soft shoes, an empty backpack, and a crowbar. It's for opening doors, not for fighting.
Inside, the shelves are almost bare. You only take what matters. Water, canned beans, and a first aid kit.
Then a shopping cart crashes over in the next aisle. Every head in the store turns toward the sound.
You don't run. Running is loud. You walk out the back door, slow and silent, while they shuffle toward the noise.
You get home with five days of water on your back. Your odds rise to sixty two.
Week one. The city has gone quiet. No traffic, no music, no planes. The living are hiding, and the dead are everywhere.
Then the smell arrives. Without power, sewer pumps stop. In San Diego's 2011 blackout, sewage started spilling within hours. Disease is now as dangerous as any bite.
You climb to the roof and look out over the city. You already know you can't stay.
Cities have the most people, the most infected, and the least food per person. Everything that kept you alive here is running out.
There's a lake an hour north. Fresh water, open views, and far fewer of them.
You leave at dawn on a bicycle. No fuel, no engine noise, and it slips between crashed cars where nothing else can.
On the road out, you hear them before you see them. A low groan, and the scrape of a thousand shoes on asphalt.
On the bridge out of town, a herd blocks the road. Hundreds of them, all shuffling east, as if they're following a sound only they can hear.
You lie in a ditch for an hour, face in the wet grass, barely breathing, until the last one passes.
On the other side, you meet five survivors heading north too. Strangers, but alive. With a group, your odds rise to sixty five.
Month one. Your group has a camp by the lake. A few tents, a fire pit, and an old canoe someone found in a boathouse.
You build a fence from pallets and car doors, hang empty cans on a wire as an alarm, and take turns on night watch.
The dangers now are small and boring. A cut that gets infected. Water someone forgot to boil. Nobody getting enough sleep.
Then one night, you wake up to the sound you hoped you'd never hear. The cans are rattling.
Twelve of them at the fence. Nobody screams. You put out every light, and someone sets a little radio playing music on the far side of the lake.
One by one, they turn and shuffle toward the music. By sunrise, they're gone. The fence held, and so did the plan.
Food is the next fight. The cans run out, so you plant potatoes and beans, and you learn to fish properly.
One afternoon, another group shows up at the crossroads. They have a nurse and a water filter. You have seeds and a mechanic.
So you trade instead of hiding. A group with a nurse, a mechanic, and a farmer is a place people will defend. Your odds climb to sixty six.
Year one. And here is the part the movies always skip.
The dead have a problem too. A body that never rests and never heals slowly falls apart in sun, rain, and frost.
The first winter freezes them in the fields like statues. By spring, the herds are slower, thinner, and fewer.
Ham radio operators link the camps together and warn each other when a herd is coming. Survivors even steer the slow herds away with noise, like shepherds.
Your camp becomes a village. Solar panels, a garden, a workshop, and a school in an old barn.
You're no longer running. You're rebuilding.
So, what were your odds?
If you jumped in your car in hour one, opened the door to your neighbor, or lit a candle on night one, the Survivometer gives you four percent.
visual: THE CAR. THE DOOR. THE CANDLE.

lines.text: If you stayed quiet, saved water, made one careful supply run, left with a group, and built a camp, your odds of seeing year one are sixty eight percent.
visual: QUIET. WATER. A GROUP. A CAMP.

lines.text: The difference was never strength. It was the small, quiet decisions you made in the first few hours.
Tell us in the comments. What's the first thing you'd grab, and who are you taking with you?
And tell us which scenario the Survivometer should run next. See you in the next what if.
